title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 15: Francisco v. House of Representatives: Constitutionality of the Davide Impeachment
keywords: Its might is in its being right
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of Francisco v. House of Representatives, the most controversial case decided by the Supreme Court during his ninth year in office, in which the Court stopped the House from acting on the second impeachment Complaint against Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr.

His narration of the facts and the Court's ruling: that the power of judicial review extends to impeachment proceedings, that 'initiate' in Article XI means to file a complaint and take initial action on it, and that Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V of the 2001 House Impeachment Rules therefore violated the one-year bar in Section 3(5).

His summary, justice by justice, of the Separate Opinions -- Bellosillo, Puno, Vitug, Santiago, Gutierrez, Callejo, Azcuna and Tinga -- setting the calls for judicial restraint against the arguments for the Court's duty to decide.

His own Concurring Opinion: why he first inhibited and was then directed to participate, why the Court's assumption of jurisdiction is mandated by the 1987 Constitution, why the House rules also violated due process, and why he rejected the Salonga-Pangalangan deferential thesis as 'passing the buck.'
sub_topics: He opens by calling the case the most controversial of his ninth year in office and credits the House's 115-77 vote on November 10, 2003, following Speaker de Venecia's ruling to respect the Decision, with averting a constitutional crisis of googolplex proportions.

He credits the Senate and Senate President Franklin Drilon for declining to interfere and President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo for steadily supporting the Court's authority as final arbiter of constitutional disputes.
The facts: the July 22, 2002 House Resolution sponsored by Representative Fuentebella directing an investigation into the Chief Justice's disbursement of the Judiciary Development Fund.

The first impeachment Complaint filed June 2, 2003 by former President Estrada against Chief Justice Davide and seven associate justices, referred to the Committee on Justice on August 5, 2003, found sufficient in form on October 13 but dismissed as insufficient in substance on October 22.

The second Complaint filed October 23, 2003 by Representatives Teodoro and Fuentebella, accompanied by an endorsement signed by at least one third of the House, and the eighteen Petitions asserting that it violated the one-year bar.

The parties' positions: the House, by special appearance through Speaker de Venecia, denying the Court's jurisdiction over a coequal branch; the Senate calling the Petitions premature; and Senator Pimentel intervening to assert the Senate's sole power to try and decide impeachment cases.

The November 5-6, 2003 Oral Argument with eight amici curiae, and the issues canvassed: standing, ripeness, political question, the House's exclusive power to initiate, the Senate's sole power to try, the constitutionality of the House Rules, and judicial restraint.

The ruling on judicial review: speaking through Justice Carpio-Morales, the Court invoked Laurel's 'moderating power' and Angara v. Electoral Commission to hold that judicial review is integral to checks and balances, reinforced by the expanded certiorari jurisdiction engraved in Section 1 of Article VIII.

The tools of constitutional construction applied -- verba legis, ratio legis est anima, and ut magis valeat quam pereat -- and the line of cases (Santiago v. Guingona, Tanada v. Angara, Bondoc v. Pineda, Coseteng v. Mitra, Daza v. Singson, Tanada v. Cuenco) showing review of congressional action.

The holdings on standing (relaxed, given expenditure of public funds and the transcendental issues), ripeness (the complaint had been filed and the rules enforced), justiciability (constitutionally imposed limits make the question examinable) and judicial restraint (adjudication could not be declined because no other tribunal could decide).

The construction of 'initiate': amicus Florenz Regalado, who had sponsored Section 3(5) as a constitutional commissioner, affirmed that initiate meant to file and to take initial action, so Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V, deeming proceedings initiated in three other ways, contravened the Constitution -- and Arroyo v. De Venecia confirmed that House rules may not ignore constitutional restraints.

The disposition: because the first Complaint was filed June 2 and referred August 5, 2003, the second Complaint of October 23, 2003 fell within the one-year bar; Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V were unconstitutional and the second Complaint barred.

The Bellosillo Opinion: judicial restraint and reasoned hesitance, a harmonious blend of courtesy and caution, and remedies to be exhausted within the legislature -- yet he too found the second Complaint constitutionally infirm.

The Puno Opinion: the issue was justiciable and impeachment sui generis, but under the 'coordinacy theory' the Court should defer until the House and Senate had acted, since wrong timing could negate the very jurisdiction claimed; he voted to dismiss.

The Vitug Concurrence: impeachment is legal and political and sui generis, and where the House transgresses the detailed constitutional procedure the issue becomes constitutional; the Court, he wrote, was probably weak but did not have to be a weakling, and the keeper of the fundamental law could not be a bystander.

His own Concurring Opinion: his initial inhibition because a petitioner was a former law partner, because amicus Salonga was a close friend, and because he was one of the eight justices charged in the first Complaint and had used JDF-funded facilities -- and the Court's October 28, 2003 Resolution directing him to participate.

The authorities on participation despite interest, drawn from amicus Bernas at the Oral Argument -- Perfecto v. Meer, Nitafan v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Abbas v. Senate Electoral Tribunal and Estrada v. Desierto -- plus the practical point that if the seven charged justices all inhibited, the Court would lose its quorum and jurisdiction.

His constitutional argument: unlike the 1935 and 1973 Constitutions and unlike the US Constitution, the 1987 charter commands the Court to strike down grave abuse of discretion by any branch, a provision authored by former Chief Justice Concepcion to remedy the judicial cop-outs of the Martial Law era, so that Philippine judges are mandated to be activists while US justices may choose between the Warren Court's activism and the Rehnquist Court's passivism.

His due process point -- the House rules are also unconstitutional insofar as they do not give the charged official notice and an opportunity to be heard -- and his Epilogue rejecting the Salonga-Pangalangan deferential thesis as 'passing the buck,' with the closing claim that the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength and that its might is in its being right.

The remaining opinions -- Santiago (defects real but resolution premature; endorsement is not filing), Gutierrez (the anti-harassment clause and the futility of misguided self-restraint), Callejo (six grounds rejecting restraint and a close parsing of 'file' versus 'initiate'), Azcuna (impeachment placed in Article XI on accountability, and proceedings occur in the House while the case is tried in the Senate) and Tinga (constitutional limits are mandatory, standing may be relaxed under Barrows v. Jackson, and the Senate cannot judge the House's rules) -- and the final 11-3-1 vote with Chief Justice Davide taking no part.

stances.claim: The Court's assumption of jurisdiction over the impeachment controversy was not optional but mandated by the 1987 Constitution, which commands it to strike down grave abuse of discretion by any branch or instrumentality of government.
stances.rhetorical_move: textual and historical argument: he contrasts the 1987 charter with the 1935, 1973 and US Constitutions and invokes Concepcion's authorship to show the provision was written precisely to end Martial Law-era evasion

stances.claim: By imposing on judges the duty to intervene and settle issues of grave abuse of discretion, the Constitution has mandated them to be activists, and a duty cannot be evaded.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty-not-power reframing: he converts what critics call activism into an obligation, so that restraint becomes dereliction

stances.claim: The deferential Salonga-Pangalangan thesis -- that the Court should let the House correct itself or let the Senate invalidate the second Complaint -- amounts to 'passing the buck' and is inconsistent with the activist duty the Constitution imposes.
stances.rhetorical_move: steelman then refusal: he sets out the advantages of the deferential position at length before rejecting it, having first admitted he was initially tempted by it

stances.claim: He could not inhibit despite his conflict of interest, because if the seven justices named in the first Complaint all withdrew the Court would lose its majority and thus its jurisdiction, and because precedent shows justices can rule against their own interests.
stances.rhetorical_move: precedent plus arithmetic: Perfecto, Nitafan, Abbas and Estrada v. Desierto establish the principle, and the count of remaining justices makes withdrawal impossible in practice

stances.claim: The judiciary's very weakness becomes its strength when it dares speak through decisions upholding the supremacy of the Constitution; its strength lies not in brute power but in moral courage, and its might is in its being right.
stances.rhetorical_move: epigrammatic close: an inversion of weakness into strength, sealed by an aphorism

notable_anecdotes: The day of the vote: he recalls that on November 10, 2003, the very day the Decision was promulgated, the House voted 115 to 77 to accept Speaker de Venecia's ruling to respect the Decision of the Supreme Court.

The crisis averted: he writes that had Congress ignored the Decision and proceeded to impeach the Chief Justice, a constitutional crisis of googolplex proportions would have ensued and the very foundation of government would have been shaken beyond imagination.

His inhibition and recall: he relates that he immediately inhibited himself because a petitioner was a former law partner and because amicus Salonga was a close friend, only to be directed by the Court's October 28, 2003 Resolution to participate.

His three conflicts named openly: that a ruling barring a second complaint would also shield him, one of the eight justices charged by Estrada; that he had used facilities bought with the JDF; and that he had voted for en banc Resolutions approving JDF expenditures.

Bernas at the Oral Argument: he recounts that on November 5, 2003 the amicus shed light on his conflict-of-interest problem by explaining Perfecto v. Meer, in which justices could rule on a judgment benefiting themselves because jurisdiction may not be declined.

Regalado's testimony on his own handiwork: the amicus who had sponsored Section 3(5) as a constitutional commissioner affirmed at the Oral Argument that 'initiate' meant to file and to take initial action, which the Court then adopted.

Vitug's line about the weakling: he records his colleague's judgment that the Court was probably weak but did not have to be a weakling, and could not afford to be a bystander watching from the sidelines.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of Francisco v. House of Representatives, which he called the most controversial case decided by the Supreme Court during his ninth year in office. The Court effectively stopped the House from acting on the second impeachment Complaint against Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide Jr., and on November 10, 2003, the day the Decision was promulgated, the House voted 115 to 77 to respect it, averting what he described as a constitutional crisis of googolplex proportions; he credited the Senate's restraint and President Arroyo's support for the outcome. He recounted the facts -- the 2002 House Resolution probing the Chief Justice's disbursement of the Judiciary Development Fund, Estrada's first impeachment Complaint of June 2, 2003 referred to the Committee on Justice on August 5 and dismissed as insufficient in substance on October 22, and the second Complaint filed the next day by Representatives Teodoro and Fuentebella -- and then the Court's ruling, delivered through Justice Carpio-Morales: judicial review extends to impeachment proceedings; standing was relaxed and the issue was ripe and justiciable; and, on the authority of amicus Florenz Regalado who had sponsored the provision, 'initiate' means to file a complaint and take initial action on it, so that Sections 16 and 17 of Rule V of the 2001 House Impeachment Rules contravened Section 3(5) of Article XI and the second Complaint was time-barred. He then summarized each Separate Opinion in order of seniority, from Bellosillo's and Puno's calls for restraint and Santiago's view that the process should first run its course, through Vitug's, Gutierrez's, Callejo's, Azcuna's and Tinga's concurrences. In his own Opinion he disclosed that he had inhibited because of a former law partner, a close friendship with amicus Salonga, and his own exposure in the first Complaint, but was directed to participate; citing Perfecto v. Meer, Nitafan, Abbas and Estrada v. Desierto, and noting that mass inhibition would strip the Court of a quorum, he argued that jurisdiction may not be declined. Because the 1987 Constitution, authored on this point by Chief Justice Concepcion to end Martial Law-era judicial cop-outs, commands judges to strike down grave abuse of discretion, he concluded that they are mandated to be activists, rejected the deferential Salonga-Pangalangan thesis as passing the buck, and closed that the judiciary's weakness becomes its strength, for its might is in its being right. The vote was 11-3-1, with Chief Justice Davide taking no part.
